To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the concept of AnGRs has been transformed from a scientific and ecological life form to a political object, which is reflected in the way in whic h AnGRs are valued today.

1) the AnGRs are today valued according to the criteria of “in-situ condition”, and not their “adaptation to local environment”, as it was in the 1990s; 2) the AnGR are today valued according their contribution to the “local economy”, and not the “national economy”, as it was during the 1980s; 3) the AnGR have today become objects of national concern, and not of international concern, as it was
the AnGR have changed from being a scientific, economic and ecologic life form into a political one and that this transformation was initiated by the adoption of the CBD and the Nagoya protocol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how the concept of AnGR has been historically transformed into political objects, and what the consequences are for their valuation and conservation.
how AnGRs have been transformed into objects of national and global concern, and how the values attached to them are today imbued in political values and national politics.
the question of how the concept of AnGRs has been transformed over time, how it is currently defined and how it is valued.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Nagoya Protocol is a political document that is not based on scientific evidence, and that it is not a legally binding document for the conservation of farm animal genetic resources.

AnGRs have become highly politicised and are now defined as a global public good that is to be managed and conserved by the sovereign powers and national governments of each party to the global conventions.
AnGRs have become political objects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how the AnGR have changed their value from natural property and global commons into objects of political concern and national property.
the Nagoya Protocol, and its underlying CBD, have transformed the nature of AnGRs from global genetic resources into national genetic resources.
the AnGRs are no longer considered a global genetic common but are rather a national genetic heritage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the values of the AnGRA are now inherently imbued in the political values of national sovereignty and the global politics of conservation.
the AnGRs have been redefined as national genetic landscapes and the Nagoya-Protocol is a legal instrument that has the potential to transform the AnGRs into national political objects.
the values of the AnGRA are not fixed but are constantly being renegotiated.
